title: Why is the Hindu number system better than the Roman?
description: Three features of our own number system are named by comparing the number 2367 in our digits and in Roman symbols. Place value, a digit for zero and column rules all make our system more convenient. The video follows the book's comparison of the Roman system.
teaching_notes: One idea: compare the two systems on the same number and look for what each feature saves. Place value needs only ten digits, zero holds an empty place, and column rules make calculation possible. Watch for students who say only that Hindu numerals look shorter.

source: Figure it Out (early number systems, question 3)
video_script.why: The child reuses the Roman landmark numbers of the solved example to see what the Hindu system does differently.
video_script.substitution: Write one number in both systems, then ask what each system needs, what it does with an empty place, and how calculation goes.

maths_rules: 2367 in the Roman system is MMCCCLXVII, which uses 10 symbols
place value: the position of a digit tells its landmark, so 10 digits write every number; Roman symbols have fixed values and need new symbols for bigger numbers
zero: our system has a digit 0 for an empty place; the Roman system has no symbol for zero
calculation: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing follow column rules in our system, while Roman numerals make them very hard
check: the three features explain why 2367 takes 4 digits in ours and 10 symbols in the Roman system
